messages.content: Calculate the standard deviation of the null hypothesis test with a sample mean of 98.2, standard deviation of 1.4, and sample size of 40 for a population mean of 98.6.

function.name: statistics_calculate_p_value
function.description: Calculate the p-value for a t-test on a single sample from a population. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

sample_mean.description: The mean of the sample data. This is a float type value.

population_mean.description: The mean of the population data. This is a float type value.

sample_std_dev.description: The standard deviation of the sample data. This is a float type value.

sample_size.description: The size of the sample data.

two_tailed.description: Whether the test is two-tailed. If not provided, default is true.

message.content:
The standard deviation you’re looking for is the **standard error of the mean** under the null hypothesis.  
It’s calculated as:

\[
SE = \frac{s}{\sqrt{n}} = \frac{1.4}{\sqrt{40}} \approx 0.22
\]

So the standard deviation (standard error) of the null‑hypothesis test is roughly **0.22**.
message.reasoning:
The user says: "Calculate the standard deviation of the null hypothesis test with a sample mean of 98.2, standard deviation of 1.4, and sample size of 40 for a population mean of 98.6."

They want the standard deviation of the null hypothesis test? That might refer to the standard error of the mean under the null hypothesis? Usually we compute the standard error: sigma / sqrt(n). But they gave sample standard deviation (1.4) and sample size 40. For a population mean of 98.6. They want the standard deviation of the null hypothesis test? Possibly they want the standard error of the sampling distribution of the sample mean under the null hypothesis. That would be sample_std_dev / sqrt(sample_size) = 1.4 / sqrt(40). Let's compute: sqrt(40) ≈ 6.3249. 1.4 / 6.3249 ≈ 0.2215. So about 0.2215.

But maybe they want the standard deviation of the test statistic? The test statistic t = (sample_mean - population_mean) / (sample_std_dev / sqrt(sample_size)). The denominator is the standard error. So the standard deviation of the test statistic under the null is sqrt((n-1)/(n-3))? Actually t distribution has variance n-1/(n-3) if df>2. But maybe they just want the standard error.

Given the phrasing: "standard deviation of the null hypothesis test" could be interpreted as the standard error of the mean under the null. So answer: 0.2215.

We can also mention that it's the standard error of the mean: 1.4 / sqrt(40) ≈ 0.2215.

Thus answer: approximately 0.22.
